radicals.meaningMnemonic: This radical has a little head, a curved abdomen, and some long, spindly antennae sticking out from its nose. There's no mistaking it — this little guy is a <radical>shrimp</radical>!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>idea</radical>.

Legs appear between two lumps of dirt. This is the earth's version of a <radical>womb</radical>. Imagine a tiny baby growing under the ground and then sprouting out, legs first, into the world. Imagine being inside this dirt womb. It's warm and damp. You feel safe.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>circle</radical>.

Just in case you don't remember this, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: What's something with <radical>nine</radical> sides? Just add a <radical>drop</radical> and you'll have something that's almost a <kanji>circle</kanji>.
This radical looks just like a <radical>roof</radical>, does it not?
This looks like a bunch of books on a shelf. It's a <radical>bookshelf</radical>!
You see three squares stacked neatly together. On closer inspection, you realize these are boxed <radical>products</radical> waiting to be shipped out.

See that cliff with the white and small bits in it? That's an <radical>original</radical> cliff — we call it that because the white and small bits are actually the bones and fossils of our planet's original inhabitants, buried in the cliffside. (And this one's got a massive sign that says "ORIGINAL," because everything's gotta be a tourist spot these days… sigh.)
You spot a wispy shape flanked by ethereal orbs of flame. Don't be scared — this is just a friendly little <radical>soul</radical> on its way to get reincarnated into a new body.

The radical is the same as the kanji, so it means <radical>body</radical>. 

Just in case you need a refresher, here's the mnemonic again: When your self goes down a slide and hits a barb, it's a painful reminder that you have a body. Sometimes people think their self is just some kind of floating, disembodied consciousness, but getting a barb stuck in oneself while going down a slide will quickly remind one of one's bodily existence.

There's a rice paddy on top of a tree… Figuratively, because trees don't bear rice, they bear <radical>fruit</radical>! Use your imagination, and those four little boxes on top of the tree kind of look like big, ripe fruits — just waiting to be picked.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>hundred</radical>.

It's kind of hard to see, but if you look at this the right way it looks like a food <radical>can</radical>. See the lid being pulled off in the top-left corner? And that horizontal line in the middle? That’s the can's label.
Someone's lying on the ground with his mouth open hoping to swallow up passers-by. This guy's a weirdo — a real <radical>creeper</radical>.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>good</radical>.

Just in case you don't remember this, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: A <radical>drop</radical> of water to a <radical>root</radical> is <kanji>good</kanji>. It's good for the roots to grow and live and thrive. And what's good for roots is good for our plants and us humans too.

This is the radical for <radical>canine</radical>, because it looks like a police dog — aka a K-9 — marching around on patrol. You can see its proud little head on the top right, its front legs below crossing as it walks, and a police vest labeled "K-9" strapped around its body. Evil-doers beware — this canine's gonna sniff you out and bring you to justice.

Alternately, you could see the F-shape on the left as a cheerful canine on its hind legs dancing with a drunkard, arm in arm as they sway along together. What a happy canine, dancing like that with a drunk person.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If you run into a <radical>gate</radical> <radical>mouth</radical> first, you’re going to have a <kanji>problem</kanji>. Smashing your mouth into a gate is going to hurt. A lot. The problem you’re now in is one of getting to a hospital and having your mouth sewn back on. The <kanji>question</kanji> is, how are you going to get to the hospital?
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine having your mouth bashed into a gate. It’s going to hurt. Imagine how painful this would be and how problematic it is. Imagine that the only question in your mind is how to get to the hospital as quickly as you possibly can.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The reason you ran mouth first into this gate was because you were being chased by a <reading>mon</reading>ster (もん). A monster in and of itself is a big enough <kanji>problem</kanji> as is, let alone smashing your mouth into a gate. You poor, hapless soul.
kanji.readingHint: Monsters are scary. Maybe you’ve had a dream where you were being chased by one. Remember how scary that is when you see this kanji.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>roof</radical> under which the <radical>leader</radical> can house one <radical>hundred</radical> of his people is at the local <kanji>lodge</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Back in the old days a lodge had to be huuuuge so when a leader brought a hundred people through town they'd have a place to stay.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>lodge</kanji> <reading>shook</reading> (しゅく) as the hundred people came tumbling in through the door. It shook, but it didn't fall over. The roof stayed firmly in place, and everyone got to sleep under it okay.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine being someone staying at the lodge as they came in and everything shook around you. This lodge would probably last through an earthquake too!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Only a <radical>tree</radical> with <radical>eye</radical>s and a <radical>heart</radical> has the ability to <kanji>imagine</kanji> and to <kanji>contemplate</kanji>. For a tree to imagine and contemplate things, it needs eyes to see and a heart to feel.
kanji.meaningHint: Can you picture a tree without eyes and a heart imagining something? Contemplating? Probably not. To imagine or contemplate, a tree definitely needs eyes to observe and a heart to experience feelings.
kanji.readingMnemonic: If a <radical>tree</radical> can <kanji>imagine</kanji>, it likely has a <reading>soul</reading> (そう). Its soul is what makes it possible for the tree to <kanji>contemplate</kanji> things, you see?
kanji.readingHint: Use your soul to imagine what this tree is imagining with its soul. Is it contemplating the deep mysteries of the universe? Is it imagining where that squirrel has gone off to?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: When a <radical>canine</radical> puts its <radical>mouth</radical> on your <radical>heart</radical>, it's a pretty unforgettable <kanji>feeling</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: The feeling is kind of hard to describe. On the one hand it's warm and loving, but on the other hand it's also kind of wet and slobbery.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Overall, though, it's a good <kanji>feeling</kanji> — so good that you feel like Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん)! With this canine lovingly slobbering on your heart, you feel like you could go out and conquer the world!
kanji.readingHint: Just be careful not to let in all the Genghis Khan feelings. The confidence and motivation are good, but the feeling of wanting to wantonly slaughter your enemies is probably one you ought to repress.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>bundle</radical> in <radical>winter</radical> is the <radical>correct</radical> way to <kanji>arrange</kanji> things. Just make sure you <kanji>organize</kanji> it all before winter comes, or it'll be too late.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture all the things you've arranged correctly ahead of winter — logs bundled for the fire, blankets for the night, and yourself, all bundled up in your neatly organized home — just as the first snowflakes begin to fall.
kanji.readingMnemonic: But the most important things to <kanji>arrange</kanji> and <kanji>organize</kanji> are your <reading>sa</reading>bers (せい). You have an extensive saber collection that you simply must organize before winter arrives.
kanji.readingHint: Last winter you tripped and fell on a saber you'd left lying around. Ouch, lesson learned. That's when your passion for organizing things in bundles started. You know better than anyone the value of arranging your sabers as safely and tidily as possible.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If the <radical>sun</radical> starts to make a <radical>sound</radical>, you know it's about to go <kanji>dark</kanji>. The sun isn't supposed to make a sound, so if you can hear it, it's probably about to fizzle out or something. After it's gone, obviously everything will be pitch black. Get ready to be in the dark!
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a weird sound coming from the sun. Maybe a rumble, or something like a balloon deflating? Then everything goes totally dark. Welp, guess you'll be living in the dark for the rest of your life.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Now wandering around your house in the <kanji>dark</kanji> you start to feel hungry, so you reach blindly for some food and take a bite. Yuck! It's <reading>an</reading>chovies (あん). You don't even like anchovies, how did they get in your house? Hmm… Dark forces are at work here…
kanji.readingHint: And because it's so dark, the anchovy taste is all you can concentrate on. Imagine that fishy, salty taste on your tongue, the little softened bones sticking between your teeth. Ugh.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
By a <radical>tree</radical>, there's a <radical>sheep</radical> in the <radical>water</radical> with a <kanji>formal name ender</kanji>. That means everyone calls him Sheep-sama. No one calls him just "Sheep," since he's kind of a big deal. He's actually like sheep royalty. When he's not in his castle, Sheep-sama enjoys playing in the water by the trees.

This can also mean <kanji>manner</kanji>, as in your manner of doing things. I guess someone with a formal name ender has a different manner of doing things.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine what Sheep-sama must have done to become such important and distinguished sheep royalty. Some pretty amazing things, probably, especially for a sheep.
kanji.readingMnemonic: This sheep with the <kanji>formal name ender</kanji> only likes to play outside in the water during the <reading>summer</reading> (さま). Summer is the best season for this fancy sheep. The other seasons just can't compare.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine playing in the water with Sheep-sama in the summer. It's crazy hot outside in the summer, so going in the water feels nice. Imagine the coolness of the refreshing water envelop your body.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: This <radical>tree</radical> must've been sent from <radical>heaven</radical>, because it has a <radical>mouth</radical> and a <radical>mustache</radical>. Like some kind of special heaven tree that talks. And why was it sent? To be a <kanji>bridge</kanji>. To be the great heavenly bridge that we all, someday, must cross.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture this majestic tree bridge laid on its side, beckoning you into heaven with its mustachioed mouth. "Cross over!" it says in its bridge voice. Do… do you just step over the mouth? Can you wipe your shoes on the mustache, like it's a bristly doormat to heaven?
kanji.readingMnemonic: Actually, to get across this <kanji>bridge</kanji> you have to give it some <reading>hash</reading> (はし) browns. That's what the bridge's mouth is for. Hash browns to get across the heaven bridge? Small price to pay, really.
kanji.readingHint: Hear the bridge shouting "HASH BROWNS" in its bridge voice. You stuff some hash into its mouth and it starts to chew loudly. Oh, ew… Little hash brown bits are getting stuck in its mustache. Fortunately, the bridge lets you across. Unfortunately, it turns out all of heaven smells like hash browns.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If you tie a <radical>thread</radical> around <radical>Wolverine</radical> and dip him in <radical>water</radical>, he'll turn <kanji>green</kanji>, like the Hulk. Some kind of weird chemical reaction. But I… I wouldn't try it if I were you. You wouldn't like him when he's green.
kanji.meaningHint: Still, imagine pulling Wolverine from X-Men out of the water with that thread, and seeing him looking kinda green. Pretty green, but he could be greener. We have to go greener! We have to make the Hulk green with envy! So you put him back in the water, again and again…
kanji.readingMnemonic: As the flailing Wolverine begins to turn even more <kanji>green</kanji>, he calls out, "HELP <reading>ME DORY</reading> (みどり)!" Me, Dory? No, not you. He's calling out to that fish from Finding Nemo, another Disney IP. "Help me Dory, I'm green!" Then Dory leaps out of the water to bite through the thread and save Wolverine… THE END. Fade to green.
kanji.readingHint: These Marvel crossovers are getting ridiculous.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Pointing a <radical>thread</radical> to the <radical>east</radical> is what you <kanji>practice</kanji> every day. You're incredibly passionate about eastward thread-pointing, so you make sure to practice every day.
kanji.meaningHint: You're absolutely obsessed with pointing your thread towards the east, so all you do is practice. Practice, practice, practice.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You do all of this <kanji>practice</kanji> to try and afford all of your <reading>ren</reading>tals (れん). One day, all of this practice will pay for all of your rentals.
kanji.readingHint: Everything in your life is a rental, so you better get to practicing. Your house, your car, your friends — all of these rentals need to be paid off!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: What you <radical>say</radical> at a <radical>temple</radical> is a <kanji>poem</kanji>. It has to be a poem, because if you say anything else it's just plain disrespectful. All of the monks and priests at this temple have to read and recite poems all day, and if they can do it forever, you can while you're visiting.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture all of the people at the temple reciting poems together. You join in too, and it's a really powerful moment!
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you recite a long <kanji>poem</kanji> at the temple you see a <reading>shee</reading>p (し) in the crowd. It's opening and closing its mouth like it wants to say the poem too.
kanji.readingHint:
You turn to the person next to you and realize you have to say everything in poem form.

Excuse me
I'm not a creep
so hear my plea
is that a sheep?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Gold</radical>, at its <radical>root</radical>, is made up of <kanji>silver</kanji>. Using silver as the root of a coin is a great way to save on gold! That's why, often, if you just scratch gold, you'll find there's silver hidden underneath, at its root.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine taking a gold coin and scrubbing it with some soap and water. As you scrub, you slowly see that it's really silver underneath. Dang it, silver again!
kanji.readingMnemonic: If you want to hunt for some <kanji>silver</kanji> for yourself, all you need is a <reading>guin</reading>ea (ぎん) pig. Guinea pigs can smell silver, so get a couple and set them loose in the woods and they'll lead you straight to it.
kanji.readingHint: Guinea pigs are to silver as normal pigs are to truffles.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> shines down on your <radical>coat rack</radical> to reveal your <radical>geoduck</radical>-patterned jacket, which then becomes the major <kanji>topic</kanji> of discussion all around town.
kanji.meaningHint: Everywhere you go, you overhear someone talking about your stylish geoduck-patterned jacket. It's the only topic anyone wants to talk about.
kanji.readingMnemonic: After a few days, the <kanji>topic</kanji> changes from the cool geoduck design to what kind of <reading>dye</reading> (だい) you used to get those real-to-life geoduck colors.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine how annoying it is to constantly be asked about the dye you used in your jacket. You'd really like to change the topic — some might even say you're dye-ing to change it…

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Eat</radical>ing the <radical>roof</radical> is a <radical>bear</radical>, because the roof is a <kanji>public building</kanji>. Because it is a public building bears are allowed to eat the roof.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a public building, like a museum or a library, and look at the roof. There's a bear eating the roof!
kanji.readingMnemonic: <kanji>Public building</kanji>s must make their roofs available for eating because of a law passed by Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん).
kanji.readingHint: Imagine Genghis Khan signing something and giving a speech talking about how important it is that all bears are able to eat the roofs of public buildings, as a bear in the background eats the roof.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>horse</radical> and a <radical>shrimp</radical> are sitting next to each other. They are both at the train <kanji>station</kanji>, waiting for a train to come and take them home.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine the horse and the shrimp sitting next to each other on a small bench. There is nobody else at the train station. It is awkward.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The train pulls into the <kanji>station</kanji>. They walk up to the train doors, but they don't open. "Perhaps <reading>a key</reading> (えき) would help?" asks the station master, as he goes over to open the door to the train.
kanji.readingHint: Instead of saying "a key" he says "eh key." How strange. Imagine the station master saying it like this with his weird accent. You ask him if he has "a key" and he replies with, "What is a key?" Then you say "eh key." He totally understands you now.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A cult <radical>leader</radical> has a great <radical>idea</radical> to recruit a <kanji>hundred million</kanji> new members. Since he’s the guy with all the ideas, he is the leader of the cult. His idea is to give every new member a free puppy. He’ll have a hundred million new recruits in no time.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a hundred million free puppies. That’s a lot. Imagine playing with all of them. You’d be pretty happy. Unless you hate puppies. Then you’d be pretty unhappy, I imagine.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The cult leader has his headquarters in <reading>Ok</reading>lahoma (おく). Are there a <kanji>hundred million</kanji> people in Oklahoma? No, probably not. But hey, this leader is shooting for the stars. First Oklahoma, then the universe!
kanji.readingHint: Picture this cult leader gathering a hundred million people into Oklahoma. It’d be awfully crowded. Imagine yourself being stifled by the bodies of a hundred million other people.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Big</radical> <radical>products</radical> need to be put in a big <kanji>container</kanji>. A small container just won’t do. These products are big and they need a big container to be contained in.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine having all these big products. How will you contain them all!? Imagine yourself stuffing all of these big products into their respective containers.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Once you get the big products into a <kanji>container</kanji>, you then lock it with a <reading>key</reading> (き). You wouldn’t want these products to bust out of their containers, so it’s best to lock them up with a key.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the size of these big keys you have to use to lock these containers. It’s a really big key. Picture yourself straining to turn the key in the lock.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>samurai</radical> radical and the <kanji>samurai</kanji> kanji are the same!
kanji.meaningHint: Know your radicals, yo!
kanji.readingMnemonic: The most famous <kanji>samurai</kanji> in Japanese history was the illustrious <reading>shee</reading>p (し) samurai. He wasn't JUST a sheep who learned the ways of the sword, he would use the wool from the sheep enemies he killed to create his armor!
kanji.readingHint: Picture the sheep samurai. Maybe draw him on a piece of paper. He's a sheep wearing wool armor, and he has ram horns on the hilt of his katana.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have a <radical>rice</radical> <radical>ladle</radical> that's specifically for paying the rice <kanji>fee</kanji>. Each scoop of something has an extra fee tacked on, so when you use a <kanji>material</kanji>, there's a fee you have to pay in that material as well.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine ladling up a nice big scoop of rice and then seeing the little fee ladle next to it. Ugh. The material fee.
kanji.readingMnemonic: One day, the <kanji>fee</kanji> ladle is suddenly the size of <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat oars! What! You're supposed to pay a row boat sized fee now?!
kanji.readingHint: That's a lot of material you have to give up every time you want to eat some rice. Maybe you should take this row boat oar ladle and row out into the ocean where no one can tax you.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You see a <radical>tree</radical> with a <radical>helicopter</radical> and a <radical>jackhammer</radical> tied to it. You look closer, because this is an odd sight, and realize that there is a sign here too. It's telling you to beware of helicopters and jackhammers in these woods. It's a poorly made <kanji>signpost</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: This is not the best signpost you've ever seen, but it's better than nothing at all, you suppose.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you look at this weird <kanji>signpost</kanji> you notice a button. You press it because it will supposedly tell you more about these dangerous helicopters and jackhammers. Instead, it just yells out in a loud obnoxious voice: <reading>HEYO</reading> (ひょう)!!
kanji.readingHint: Press it a few more times and hear the sound in your head. Also spell it out in kana as you hear it as a nice little additional visual.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's <radical>treasure</radical> in this <radical>tree</radical> so you take out your <radical>weapon</radical> and <kanji>kill</kanji> it.
kanji.meaningHint: You didn't just cut the tree down, you stabbed it and sliced it and killed it to death.
kanji.readingMnemonic: But after the <kanji>kill</kanji>, <reading>Satsu</reading>ki (さつ) appears and yells at you. She likes trees — remember how she protected one in the 札 mnemonic? — so Satsuki's pretty upset you'd kill one like that.
kanji.readingHint: Here's that little girl Satsuki again. Remember how you imagined her last time? Try to have a picture of her in your mind so these さつ kanji are easier to remember.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Under a misshapen crescent <radical>moon</radical>, a <radical>dog</radical> <radical>boil</radical>s as much <kanji>nature</kanji> as it can find.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a weird-looking, misshapen crescent moon casting its light onto the scene of a dog boiling up everything you'd find in nature. Trees, sticks, mud, little animals. All of that is being boiled by this dog by the light of a weird-looking moon.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Destroying <kanji>nature</kanji> like this is the dog's way of practicing <reading>Zen</reading> (ぜん) Buddhism. As it breathes in the fumes from all of the different pieces of nature being boiled down, the dog gets really zen and chill.
kanji.readingHint: Picture the dog kneeling in front of the pot of concentrated nature and breathing deeply as it practiced Zen. You kind of wish you could join it, considering how peaceful it looks.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Your <radical>womb</radical> spins in a <radical>circle</radical> and starts to <radical>boil</radical> with <kanji>heat</kanji>. Uh oh, I think you have a <kanji>fever</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Even if you don't have a womb, just picture one anyway: it's turning around in a circle faster and faster, as the heat bubbles and boils in you. You can feel this heat spread through your entire body as you burn up with a fever.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>heat</kanji> from your <kanji>fever</kanji> is making your insides and your head and your entire body spin and boil, until your doctor throws some <reading>nets</reading> (ねつ) around you. You were flailing around and they couldn't get you to stop, so they had to catch you in a series of nets.
kanji.readingHint: These nets aren't making the fever heat go away, but they have made the spinning stop at least.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: I always <radical>say</radical> the <radical>fruit</radical> <kanji>section</kanji> at the grocery should be at the front of the store. It’s the perfect place for the fruit section, I say.
kanji.meaningHint: Think about it. Every grocery store has the fruit section right at the front, wouldn’t you say?
kanji.readingMnemonic: To get to the fruit <kanji>section</kanji>, you have to go to the store. To get to the store you have to drive a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). Driving a car is the fastest way to get to the fruit section at the store.
kanji.readingHint: Picture yourself driving a car and salivating over the fruit waiting for you in the fruit section. Imagine your favorite fruit as you put the pedal to the metal in your awesome car.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>Viking</radical> opens his <radical>mouth</radical>, and below it, a <radical>shellfish</radical> sits. Grab that shellfish and throw it into his mouth to win a <kanji>prize</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a game at a fair where you have to throw a shellfish into the mouth of a hungry Viking. You want this prize just as much as the Viking wants his shellfish.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>prize</kanji> you're working so hard to win is lunch with the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう). This is a pretty huge prize, considering all you're doing is knocking something over.
kanji.readingHint: You want this prize. You want to meet the Shougun. Soon you'll both be eating shellfish together!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: For your <radical>car</radical> you use a <radical>hat</radical>, some <radical>ground</radical> and a <radical>bookshelf</radical> to build a new <kanji>wheel</kanji>. I mean, it's generally <kanji>ring</kanji> and <kanji>loop</kanji> shaped, it just needs to be a <kanji>circle</kanji>, so it should work, right?
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine this wheel you made out of a hat, some ground (presumably to keep it all together), and a bookshelf. You install it on your car and hope for the best. This is why you should buy wheels from professional wheel makers.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Your <kanji>wheel</kanji> is... generally <reading>rin</reading>g (りん) shaped, so that's good.
kanji.readingHint: A ring-shaped wheel is better than nothing. Hopefully it will get you where you need to go.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You want to get a <radical>scooter</radical>, so you have one self (<radical>oneself</radical>) and another self working <radical>together</radical> to <kanji>choose</kanji>. The two tiny yous sit on each of your shoulders, like angel and devil, and argue about which scooter you should choose.
kanji.meaningHint: Your angel self says you should choose the safest scooter. The devil self says safety is for suckers, and you should buy one that's loud and dangerous and covered in flames.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Suddenly your selfs both gasp and <kanji>choose</kanji> a scooter in front of you that looks like a <reading>cen</reading>taur (せん). The scooter is designed like a human on the top, the bars are its arms, and the bottom with the seat and the wheels are all horse. This centaur scooter is what you choose to ride.
kanji.readingHint: The angel self says, "I choose this centaur scooter because of its strong arms." The devil self says, "I choose this scooter because it looks like a badass horse monster, wooh!"

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Gold</radical> reveals itself when you <radical>stand</radical> and <radical>see</radical> into this <kanji>mirror</kanji>. Yes, even you are made of gold. You're so great and valuable, standing in front of that mirror. It's not hard to see, especially in a mirror – you're golden.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine looking at yourself in the mirror only to see you're made of gold. It would be pretty shocking. Imagine how surprised you would be.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you look into the <kanji>mirror</kanji> you think, "<reading>Kaga</reading>… <reading>me</reading> (かがみ)?" You always forget that you're Chairman Kaga from the Iron Chef TV show. That's why you say "Kaga… me?" every time you look in the mirror.
kanji.readingHint: Picture yourself in front of a mirror, except your reflection is Chairman Kaga Takeshi. (Look up his picture if it helps.) Imagine not recognizing yourself at first, how weird that would feel, then suddenly remembering: "Kaga… me!"

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Sheep</radical> <radical>fins</radical> are <radical>good</radical> for <kanji>foster</kanji> children. The sheep have been genetically combined with fish, so the sheep have fins (and they've lost their tails — which is why the tail part of the sheep radical is missing in this kanji). These sheep fins are rich in nutrients, so they're good for fostering big, strong foster children.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine eating a fish fin with sheep wool on it. It tastes fishy like the ocean but the wool tastes like clothes. It's probably the worst thing ever, but try to imagine you're tasting it right now.

vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

Just like you can say あったかい for 温かい, people often say あっためる in conversation. The "official" reading is still あたためる, so when typing out the kanji or taking a test, try to stick to あたためる.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>arrange</kanji> something according to <kanji>reason</kanji>, the result is an <vocabulary>arrangement</vocabulary>.

vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

You know this verb is for when you are doing the solving because you think it's super <reading>coo</reading>' (く) to solve things.

vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>separate</kanji>, so you can guess the meaning is <vocabulary>to separate</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be divided</vocabulary>.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This is the same as 共有 but the verb version.

vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: How can you solve your <kanji>study</kanji> <kanji>problem</kanji>? With a little extra <vocabulary>schooling</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>study</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>learning</vocabulary>.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji 受 means accept and this verb is related. It means to get accepted, usually into something good like a university or a new job. It can also mean to pass, often in the context of a test or an exam. This is an intransitive verb, so no direct object is needed. A hint for this is that it ends with okurigana that rhyme with ある, and those kinds of verbs tend to be intransitive. Also, be careful: in English you'd use the transitive expression "pass a test," but in Japanese you'd say 試験に受かる. Kind of like saying you pass in the exam — so it's still intransitive!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. Here's a little mnemonic to help ya remember:

<vocabulary>To get accepted</vocabulary> into this program, you have to juggle <reading>u</reading>nis (う)—yes, those spiky sea urchins! Handling uni is tough, but if you want <vocabulary>to pass</vocabulary> the test and get accepted, you've got to master the uni challenge.

Who predicted the discovery of <vocabulary>Uranus</vocabulary>? <reading>No</reading>stradamus (のう), of course!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You have the kanji for <kanji>empty</kanji>, so this verb means <vocabulary>to become empty</vocabulary>. Think empty bottles, vacant bathroom stalls, even an open block in your schedule — that sort of thing.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Whenever something is about <vocabulary>to become empty</vocabulary>, you can't help saying "<reading>Ah</reading> (あ)…" to express your disappointment. Your glass of water is becoming empty? Ah… Your bag of chips is becoming empty? Ah… Exclaiming a little "Ah…" is the only thing that helps you cope with the sadness of your favorite things becoming empty.

Note that this word can also be read as すく in some situations, though the nuance changes slightly. You'll learn this through other words later on, so for now just focus on the あく reading!
